hook.support: You're making a video. You grab a photo, a song and some facts from the internet. Who owns them? Can you just use them?
hook.core: You're making a video for your VM project. You grab a photo from a search, a trending song for the background, and a few facts from a website. It looks great. But who owns that photo? That song? Those words? And what happens if you use them without asking?

why.support: Most things online are owned by someone. That's **copyright**. Learn when you can use other people's work, and how to give **credit**.
why.core: Almost everything online, from photos and songs to articles and videos, is owned by someone. That's **copyright**. Using other people's work isn't always wrong, but you need to know when you're allowed to, and how to give **credit** properly. Get it right, and your work is honest and professional. Get it wrong, and you could lose marks, have your video taken down, or even end up in court.
why.extend: Copyright protects creators' rights in their work, and the conventions of attribution let others build on that work honestly. Knowing what's protected, when use is permitted (licences, Creative Commons, fair dealing), and how to reference sources is essential for creating digital content at school, in training and at work.

articles.title: Credit where it's due

body.support:
Most things online belong to someone.

**Copyright** is automatic in Australia. When someone makes a photo, song or video, they own it.

**When can you use it?**

- When you have **permission**.
- When it has a **Creative Commons** licence. Follow its rules.
- For some school uses, like study or a review. Use only a small part, and give credit.
- When it's **your own** photo or music.

**Give credit with TASL:**

- **T**itle: what it's called
- **A**uthor: who made it
- **S**ource: where you found it
- **L**icence: the licence.

*“Sunset at Lorne” by J. Lee, Flickr, CC BY 2.0.*

For facts, write down who wrote it and the link.
body.core:
When you make a video, poster or post, it's easy to grab photos, music and facts from the internet. But most things online belong to someone.

**What is copyright?** In Australia, **copyright** is automatic. When someone makes a photo, song, article, video or drawing, they own it. They don't have to sign up or put a © on it. It usually lasts until 70 years after the maker dies. The owner decides who can copy, share or change their work.

**When can you use other people's work?**

- **With permission.** Ask the owner, and keep their reply.
- **With a licence.** A **Creative Commons** licence says *you can use this, if you follow the rules*. Lots of photos, songs and videos have one. Look for **BY** (give credit), **NC** (not for money), **ND** (don't change it) and **SA** (share yours the same way).
- **Fair dealing.** The law lets you use *some* of a work for a few reasons. These are study, review, parody and news. You don't need to ask. But use only what's fair. For review and news, you must give credit.
- **Your own work.** Your own photos, drawings and recordings are always safe to use.

**How to give credit.** For Creative Commons work, use **TASL**:

- **T**itle: what it's called
- **A**uthor: who made it
- **S**ource: where you found it (with a link)
- **L**icence: which licence it uses.

*Example: “Sunset at Lorne” by J. Lee, Flickr, CC BY 2.0.*

For facts and quotes, add a **reference**: who wrote it, the title, the date and the link.

**Why it matters.** Giving credit is honest. It shows where your facts came from. If you ignore copyright, you could lose marks for **plagiarism**. Your video could be muted or taken down. A business could end up in court.
body.extend:
Digital content is easy to copy. But most of it is protected by **copyright**.

**Copyright in Australia** starts the moment an original work is made. That covers photos, songs, texts, films and artwork. You don't need to register it or add a © symbol. It usually lasts until 70 years after the creator dies. Only the owner can copy, share or adapt the work, or let others do so.

**Lawful use of others' work**

- **Permission** from the owner, ideally in writing.
- **Licences**, such as **Creative Commons**. Creators give permission in advance, on set conditions: **BY** (credit me), **NC** (not for profit), **ND** (no changes), **SA** (share alike).
- **Fair dealing.** The Copyright Act allows limited use without asking, for set purposes. These include research or study, criticism or review, parody or satire, and news. The use must be fair in amount and purpose. Review and news also need credit. Australia's rule is narrower than the US idea of *fair use*.
- **Original work** you make yourself.

**How to credit.** For Creative Commons work, use **TASL**: **T**itle, **A**uthor, **S**ource (with a link) and **L**icence. *“Sunset at Lorne” by J. Lee, Flickr, CC BY 2.0.* For facts and quotes, give a **reference**: author, title, date and source.

**What's at stake.** Not giving credit is **plagiarism** at school and in training. Breaking copyright can get your content removed. It can also lead to court, and to paying damages or royalties.

caseStudies.title: The kookaburra in Down Under

body.support:
**Down Under** is a famous Australian song from the 1980s. It has a catchy **flute tune**.

A company owned the rights to the kids' song **Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree**. It said the flute tune copied part of Kookaburra. It went to **court**.

In **2010**, the judge agreed. Just a few notes were copied. But it was enough.

The owners of Down Under had to pay **5%** of the song's money to the Kookaburra owners.

The lesson: even a few notes can be protected. Check, and give credit.
body.core:
**Down Under** by Men at Work is one of Australia's best-known songs. It was a number one hit in the early 1980s. It has a catchy **flute riff**.

A company called **Larrikin Music** owned the copyright in the kids' song **Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree**. Years later, it said the flute riff copied part of Kookaburra. It took the case to the **Federal Court**.

In **February 2010**, the judge agreed. He found the riff copied a **big enough part** of Kookaburra. It wasn't the whole song. It was just a few bars, with other music in between. But it was enough.

In **July 2010**, the court decided what Larrikin should get. Larrikin had asked for up to **60%** of the song's royalties. The judge said that was far too much. He gave Larrikin **5%**, from 2002 and into the future.

The other side appealed. In **2011**, a higher court agreed with the judge.

The lesson: even a few notes from a famous song can be protected. If it's not yours, check, and credit.
body.extend:
**Down Under**, by Men at Work, topped the charts in the early 1980s. It became an unofficial Australian anthem, partly because of its **flute riff**.

**Larrikin Music** owned the copyright in the children's song **Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree**. It claimed the riff copied part of that song, and sued in the **Federal Court**.

In **February 2010**, Justice Jacobson agreed. The riff copied a **substantial part** of Kookaburra. Yet the borrowed part was short. It was split in two, with other music in between, so it was hard to hear. Copying a whole work isn't needed. A substantial part is enough, judged by quality as well as amount.

In **July 2010**, the court set the payment. Larrikin had asked for up to **60%** of royalties. The judge called that excessive. He awarded **5%** of the song's income from 2002 onwards. An appeal failed in **2011**.

The case shows that copyright protects small but clear parts of a work. The cost can follow a creator for decades.

teacher.overview: Students learn the principles of copyright in Australia (automatic protection, owners' rights), lawful ways to use others' work (permission, licences including Creative Commons, fair dealing, original work), and the conventions of attribution (TASL: title, author, source, licence) and referencing. They plan and make a short digital text using only content they're allowed to use, with a full credits section. The case study is the 2010 Federal Court finding that Down Under's flute riff reproduced a substantial part of Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree.
prep: Have links ready to Creative Commons search tools and free media libraries (Wikimedia Commons, Free Music Archive, Unsplash), checked on school devices.
Decide the format for the Do it (slideshow, poster, short video, web page).
Optional: play Down Under and Kookaburra so students can hear the riff.

keyPoints: Copyright in Australia is automatic; it usually lasts until 70 years after the creator's death.
You can use others' work with permission, under a licence (e.g. Creative Commons), under fair dealing for limited purposes, or if it's your own.
Creative Commons elements: BY (credit), NC (non-commercial), ND (no changes), SA (share alike).
Credit with TASL: title, author, source, licence; reference facts with who, title, date and link.
Fair dealing (research or study, criticism or review, parody or satire, news) is narrower than US fair use, and some purposes require acknowledgement.
Down Under (2010): a substantial part, even a short riff, can infringe copyright.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** the legal right to own and control your creative work; it starts automatically when the work is created. Permission, a licence (e.g. Creative Commons), fair dealing for limited purposes, or your own work. Title, Author, Source, Licence.

**Credits:** 1 title; 2 author; 3 source; 4 licence; 5 music credit; 6 reference for information.

**Sort:** own photo — yes; CC BY Flickr photo — yes, with credit; downloaded hit song — no; council facts — yes, with credit; news photo, no licence — no; CC BY-ND track played as is — yes, with credit.

**Write the credits:** “Run Wild” by Mila Grey, Free Music Archive, CC BY 4.0 · “City Lights” by Ava Kim, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 · WorkSafe Victoria, “Working at heights”, accessed [date], [link].

**Case study:** the flute riff reproduced a substantial part of Kookaburra, so it infringed copyright; Larrikin was awarded 5% of royalties from 2002. Even a small, recognisable part can be protected. Your video could be muted or taken down, you could lose marks, or the owner could take action.

realityCheck: **Students think “online” means “free”.** The sort activity challenges this directly.
**Schools have special licences.** Some uses are covered by the education statutory licence; check Smartcopying, but students still need to credit.
**Music is the hardest.** Point students to Creative Commons or royalty-free libraries, or have them make their own.
**Keep it practical.** The goal isn't to scare students but to build honest, professional habits.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It sets up Make a Podcast, where students will need to credit everything they use.
